title: $148,061,628, Not $600 Million: the CIA Cloud Contract as the Court of Federal Claims Recorded It

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The figures are in the published opinion, and they are not the figures in circulation: "AWS's total evaluated price was $148,061,628 and IBM's total evaluated price was $93,917,785." The Source Selection Authority chose the dearer bid on the record: "I do not believe that the $54 million difference, over five years, outweighs Amazon's strengths — specifically their superior technical solution." One pricing detail cut the other way: "IBM proposed a guaranteed minimum of $39 million, as compared to AWS's guaranteed minimum of $25 million", IBM's being "nearly double the anticipated Year 1 amount for IBM's services".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise is the shape of the thing bought. The RFP "called for an established cloud service provider to build a custom clone of its public cloud for the agency", as a single indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity award with "an initial five-year ordering period, a three-year option, and a two-year option" — ten years of potential dependence on one vendor's architecture, with a pass/fail gate requiring "an existing, large-scale public offering" that only a handful of firms could clear.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog in this record is partly the court's own. This is the redacted public version — "Redactions are indicated by [¶]... ]" — and one Scenario 5 price appears as "approximately $[...]". It is also the fog the protest itself created: AWS objected to re-competing "especially where so much information has been released to IBM during the debriefing process", and the court agreed that "the winner must resubmit a new proposal with the information from its original offer already disclosed. In effect, AWS would have to bid against its own winning proposal."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the contract, awarded 14 February 2013 after an evaluation in which the agency "deemed Amazon's proposal superior to IBM's proposal in every category except management", with overall proposal risk rated "low" for Amazon and "high" for IBM. The court's summary: "AWS's offer was superior, and the outcome of the competition was not even close."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The stage that failed is the review, and the court says so of the reviewer. It held "that the GAO's decision recommending corrective action lacks a rational basis", because "the GAO completely overlooked the question of whether IBM suffered any prejudice and had standing to bring the protest in the first place" — the decision "does not even mention the existence of any 'prejudice' to IBM". The administrative record ran to "14 volumes and 13,048 pages". Declaratory relief was granted and no injunction entered, because the contract was already being performed.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Competition in Contracting Act's automatic stay on a protested award, 31 U.S.C. § 3553(d)(3), which the agency overrode to let performance proceed, and the GAO bid-protest forum whose recommendations an agency may follow — a structure in which, as the Federal Circuit has held, "an agency's decision lacks a rational basis if it implements a GAO recommendation that is itself irrational."
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A published holding that a losing offeror's manufactured protest ground cannot support corrective action where it had no chance of winning, and that reopening a competition after a debriefing is itself a prejudice to the winner. The practical effect was a ten-year single-vendor intelligence cloud, performed from February 2013 onward.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A pass/fail gate requiring an existing large-scale public cloud limits the field to incumbents; the winner's proposal is disclosed to the loser at debriefing; the loser protests; corrective action would make the winner re-bid against its own disclosed offer; so the protest process itself becomes a transfer from winner to loser unless a court stops it. The court stopped it, and the incumbency stood.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Amazon was handed a $600 million CIA cloud contract on the strength of family ties to the national-security state — Jeff Bezos's grandfather's career at ARPA and the Atomic Energy Commission — rather than on the merits.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: THE FULL TEXT OF THE PUBLISHED OPINION WAS SEARCHED, AND NEITHER NAME NOR NUMBER IS IN IT. "Bezos" does not appear. "Gise" does not appear. There is no reference to ARPA, to DARPA, to the Atomic Energy Commission, or to anyone's family. And the figure "600" appears nowhere: the price before the court was "AWS's total evaluated price was $148,061,628", against IBM's $93,917,785 — a five-year evaluated figure, not six hundred million. Whatever the source of the circulating number, it is not this record, and this dossier does not repeat it. What the record shows instead is a competitive best-value procurement that the dearer bidder won on technical merit, with the agency rating Amazon superior "in every category except management" and its overall risk "low" against IBM's "high", and a Source Selection Authority who wrote down why the $54 million premium was worth paying. THE PART OF THE RECORD THAT INVERTS THE STORY'S MORAL is what the court found about the loser. In its own voice, not a party's: "the GAO failed to address the way in which IBM manipulated its pricing to create a bid protest issue. IBM appears to have intentionally manufactured a protest argument relating to the Scenario 5 pricing requirement, which it hoped to pursue if it lost the C2S competition with AWS. Knowing full well from its pre-proposal questions what the Scenario 5 requirements were, IBM drastically departed from the approach followed in its initial proposal when it came to submitting its final proposal revision ... IBM was the only offeror who appeared to 'misunderstand' the Scenario 5 pricing requirements, as the other offerors all interpreted Scenario 5 in the same way. IBM strongly disagrees that it manipulated the procurement in this manner, but the Court does not see any other explanation for IBM's final pricing strategy." The insider move the legend attributes to the winner, the court attributes to the incumbent that lost. WHAT THIS DOSSIER STILL CANNOT SAY: the GAO's own decision of 6 June 2013 was not read, only the court's account of it; the opinion is redacted and some prices are withheld; and nothing here speaks to what the contract was used for, what the ten-year total came to, or any later award.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Amazon Web Services, Inc. v. The United States, and IBM U.S. Federal, Defendant-Intervenor, 113 Fed. Cl. 102, No. 13-506C (U.S. Court of Federal Claims; sealed 31 October 2013, reissued for publication 8 November 2013). It records: a Central Intelligence Agency competitive acquisition for cloud computing services known as C2S; an RFP issued 15 June 2012 calling for an established cloud service provider to build a custom clone of its public cloud for the agency, as a single IDIQ award with an initial five-year ordering period plus three-year and two-year options; evaluation on a best-value basis across technical/management, past performance, security, price and risk, with a pass/fail gate requiring an existing large-scale public cloud offering; an evaluation deeming Amazon superior in every category except management, with risk rated low for Amazon and high for IBM; total evaluated prices of $148,061,628 for AWS and $93,917,785 for IBM, guaranteed minimums of $25 million and $39 million respectively, and a Source Selection Authority finding the $54 million difference over five years outweighed by Amazon's superior technical solution; award to AWS on 14 February 2013; IBM's GAO protest of 26 February 2013, the agency's override of the CICA automatic stay, and the GAO's decision of 6 June 2013 sustaining the protest in part and recommending corrective action; AWS's suit of 24 July 2013; an administrative record of 14 volumes and 13,048 pages; and a holding that the GAO's decision lacks a rational basis because it overlooked prejudice and standing, that IBM had no chance of winning, that IBM appears to have intentionally manufactured the Scenario 5 protest argument, and that reopening the competition would require the winner to bid against its own disclosed proposal. Declaratory relief granted; no injunction entered.

citations.title: Amazon Web Services, Inc. v. The United States, and IBM U.S. Federal, Defendant-Intervenor, 113 Fed. Cl. 102, No. 13-506C (U.S. Court of Federal Claims; filed under seal 31 October 2013, reissued for publication 8 November 2013) (Wheeler, J.)
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full on CourtListener in a browser (courtlistener.com returns an empty HTTP 202 for opinion URLs to scripted requests, so link checks may report this blocked). The opinion is the published, redacted version: "Redactions are indicated by [¶]... ]." THE PROCUREMENT: "This post-award bid protest arises from a competitive acquisition by the Central Intelligence Agency ('the agency') for cloud computing services ('C2S')." The RFP issued 15 June 2012 and "called for an established cloud service provider to build a custom clone of its public cloud for the agency", as "a single indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity ('IDIQ') cloud computing contract" with "ten years" of potential performance — "an initial five-year ordering period, a three-year option, and a two-year option". Award was on a "best value" basis across technical/management, past performance, security, price and (added by amendment) risk. THE NUMBERS, WHICH ARE IN THE PUBLISHED OPINION: "AWS's total evaluated price was $148,061,628 and IBM's total evaluated price was $93,917,785." The Source Selection Authority's trade-off, quoted by the court: "Amazon's price is $148,061,628, while IBM's is $93,917,785 ... I do not believe that the $54 million difference, over five years, outweighs Amazon's strengths — specifically their superior technical solution." Also: "IBM proposed a guaranteed minimum of $39 million, as compared to AWS's guaranteed minimum of $25 million", IBM's figure being "nearly double the anticipated Year 1 amount for IBM's services". The agency "deemed Amazon's proposal superior to IBM's proposal in every category except management, and except for 'security' where each proposal received a 'pass' rating", and rated overall proposal risk "low" for Amazon and "high" for IBM. The contract was awarded to AWS on 14 February 2013. THE PROTEST AND WHAT THE COURT MADE OF IT: IBM protested at the GAO on 26 February 2013; the agency overrode the CICA automatic stay; the GAO sustained the protest in part on 6 June 2013 and recommended corrective action (IBM U.S. Federal, B-407073.3 et al., 2013 CPD ¶ 142 (Comp. Gen. June 6, 2013)); AWS sued on 24 July 2013. The administrative record ran to "14 volumes and 13,048 pages". The court held "that the GAO's decision recommending corrective action lacks a rational basis, and therefore that the agency's decision to follow the GAO's recommendation also lacks a rational basis", because "the GAO completely overlooked the question of whether IBM suffered any prejudice and had standing to bring the protest in the first place". THE FINDING ABOUT THE PROTESTOR, stated by the court in its own voice: "the GAO failed to address the way in which IBM manipulated its pricing to create a bid protest issue. IBM appears to have intentionally manufactured a protest argument relating to the Scenario 5 pricing requirement, which it hoped to pursue if it lost the C2S competition with AWS. Knowing full well from its pre-proposal questions what the Scenario 5 requirements were, IBM drastically departed from the approach followed in its initial proposal when it came to submitting its final proposal revision. If it did not win the award, IBM could argue that the agency did not evaluate Scenario 5 prices on a common basis. IBM was the only offeror who appeared to 'misunderstand' the Scenario 5 pricing requirements, as the other offerors all interpreted Scenario 5 in the same way. IBM strongly disagrees that it manipulated the procurement in this manner, but the Court does not see any other explanation for IBM's final pricing strategy." THE CONCLUSION: "There is no such thing as a perfect procurement"; "IBM never met that burden, and the GAO neglected to address it"; "AWS's offer was superior, and the outcome of the competition was not even close"; and on the remedy sought, "The unfairness inherent in such an action is that the winner must resubmit a new proposal with the information from its original offer already disclosed. In effect, AWS would have to bid against its own winning proposal. This Court will not allow such an unjust result." Declaratory relief was granted; no injunction was entered. WHAT THE FULL TEXT DOES NOT CONTAIN, CHECKED BY SEARCH: the figure "600" appears nowhere in it, and neither does "Bezos" nor "Gise". There is no reference to any family connection, to ARPA or DARPA, or to anyone's lineage. The $600 million figure attached to this contract in public discussion is not a number in this record; the evaluated price before the court was $148,061,628. The GAO's own 6 June 2013 decision was not read — only the court's account of it.
